(CNN) — On Sunday, Democratic White House hopeful Barack Obama pushed back against claims that he and his wife, Michelle, lacked patriotism.

Speaking after a town hall event in Lorain, Ohio, Obama was questioned by a reporter about what was described as an effort by conservatives and Republicans to portray him as unpatriotic. The reporter pointed to a past occasion when Obama did not place his hand over his heart during the national anthem.

Obama responded that if failing to do so were grounds for disqualification, then “about three-quarters” of people who had ever attended a football or baseball game would also be disqualified.

The reporter also raised several other issues: Obama’s decision not to wear an American flag pin on his lapel, his contact with former members of the Weather Underground, a radical anti-Vietnam War organization, and a recent remark by Michelle Obama that she had not felt truly proud of the United States until lately.

Asked how he planned to counter the perception that he was unpatriotic, Obama said general elections always involve “some nonsense.” He noted that earlier criticism had focused on his name, then on false e-mails claiming he was Muslim, and now on questions about his patriotism.

Obama said his answer would be to tell the truth: that everything he had become was because of the United States.

The Illinois senator, then in his first term, had faced a number of false rumors since beginning his presidential campaign. Those included claims that he was Muslim, that he had taken his oath of office on the Quran, and that, as a child in Indonesia, he had attended a radical Islamic school.

Obama reminded reporters that he first gained national prominence because of a speech in which he talked about his affection for America.

He also addressed Michelle Obama’s controversial comment, saying she had already clarified what she meant. According to Obama, she had simply misspoken and had intended to say that this was the first time she had felt proud of American politics.

He said many people who had grown skeptical or disappointed with politics could relate to that feeling. Michelle Obama, he added, had often spoken about being cynical toward American politics for a long time, but was now encouraged by the way people were becoming active and engaged in ways not seen for many years.

On the issue of not wearing a flag pin, Obama argued that Republicans did not have exclusive ownership of patriotism. He criticized a party that, in his view, had overseen a war in which troops lacked needed body armor, sent poorly trained forces into combat because of bad planning, failed to provide adequate veterans’ benefits after service members returned home, and weakened the Constitution through unnecessary warrantless wiretapping.

Obama said he welcomed a debate over that record and wanted to see what Americans considered the real meaning of patriotism.

He did not answer the question about the Weather Underground, whose members bombed the U.S. Capitol and the Pentagon in the 1970s.

The previous week, the New York Sun reported that in 2001, while serving as an Illinois state senator, Obama accepted a $200 donation from William Ayers, a founder of the Weather Underground. Ayers was not convicted in connection with the bombings and later became a professor at the University of Illinois at Chicago.

According to the paper, Obama campaign spokesman William Burton said in a statement that Obama “strongly condemns” the violent acts committed by the Weathermen, as he condemns all violence. Burton added that Obama had been only 8 years old when Ayers and the Weathermen were active, and that any effort to link Obama to events from nearly four decades earlier was absurd.

Former first lady and Sen. Hillary Clinton had repeatedly argued that she was the stronger Democratic candidate because she had already demonstrated an ability to endure attacks from conservatives.

**Obama pushes back on GOP attacks over patriotism**

**COLUMBUS, Ohio (CNN)** — Sen. Barack Obama on Tuesday forcefully defended himself and his wife, Michelle, against Republican criticism questioning their patriotism, accusing GOP opponents of trying to distract voters from the issues dominating the 2008 presidential campaign.

Speaking to reporters while campaigning in Ohio, the Democratic presidential contender said attacks on his patriotism — and recent criticism of his wife — were part of a familiar political playbook.

“Let me just be absolutely clear: I am proud of my country,” Obama said. “I love this country, and so does Michelle.”

The controversy intensified after Michelle Obama told a Wisconsin crowd that “for the first time in my adult lifetime, I am really proud of my country,” citing what she described as a surge of civic engagement around her husband’s campaign. Republicans quickly seized on the remark, arguing it suggested a lack of pride in the United States.

Obama said his wife’s comments had been distorted.

“What she meant was that she was proud of the fact that people are getting involved in the political process in a way that she hadn’t seen before,” he said. “Anybody who tries to suggest otherwise is just playing politics.”

The Illinois senator also responded to criticism from conservatives over his decision not to routinely wear an American flag lapel pin, an issue that had resurfaced repeatedly during the campaign. Obama has said he stopped wearing the pin after the September 11 attacks became, in his view, a substitute for “true patriotism,” which he defined as speaking honestly about the country’s challenges and working to improve it.

Republican strategists and conservative commentators have used both issues to raise questions about Obama’s values as he seeks to become the nation’s first Black president. Obama said he expected such attacks to continue if he became the Democratic nominee.

“If they think that they’re going to somehow make me into someone who doesn’t love this country, they’re mistaken,” he said. “I’ve been fighting for this country my entire adult life — fighting to expand opportunity, fighting for working families, fighting to make sure America lives up to its ideals.”

The exchange came as Obama and Sen. Hillary Clinton battled for delegates in a tightening Democratic primary race, with Ohio and Texas emerging as crucial contests. Obama has built his campaign around opposition to the Iraq war, calls for political change and appeals to voters disillusioned with Washington.

Republicans, meanwhile, have begun sharpening their criticism of Obama as he has gained momentum. Sen. John McCain, the likely Republican nominee, has largely avoided direct personal attacks on Obama’s patriotism, though some Republican allies have signaled that questions about Obama’s background and statements by his wife could become part of the general-election debate.

Obama said voters were more concerned about the economy, the war in Iraq, health care and government ethics than political arguments over symbols.

“The American people are smarter than that,” he said. “They understand that patriotism is not about what pin you wear or what slogan you repeat. It’s about whether you are committed to making this country better.”

Michelle Obama’s remarks have also drawn scrutiny because of her increasingly prominent role on the campaign trail. A Harvard-trained lawyer and former hospital executive, she has become one of her husband’s most visible advocates, often speaking about student loans, family pressures and the aspirations of working parents.

Obama said he would not allow attacks on his wife to go unanswered.

“She is the best person I know,” he said. “She has worked hard, she has served her community, and she loves this country deeply. I’m not going to let anybody distort her words or question her character.”

The controversy underscored the broader challenge facing Obama as he attempted to maintain his message of unity while responding to intensifying partisan attacks. His campaign has argued that the criticism reflects old-style politics — the kind Obama says his candidacy is designed to overcome.

“This is exactly what people are tired of,” Obama said. “They want a politics that brings people together and deals with the problems we face. That’s the campaign I’m running.”

**REPORTER:**  
The issue has become personal for the Obama campaign, with advisers saying Michelle Obama has been unfairly portrayed. Obama argued that spouses should not be used as political targets and said the campaign should remain focused on the problems facing voters.

Questions of patriotism have also surfaced over Obama’s decision at times not to wear an American flag lapel pin. The senator has said he respects the flag but does not believe patriotism should be reduced to a symbol.

**OBAMA:**  
I revere the flag. I honor the men and women who serve under it. But wearing a pin is not a substitute for supporting veterans, restoring America’s standing in the world, and making sure our government lives up to our values. Patriotism is what you do, not just what you wear.

**REPORTER:**  
That explanation has not stopped critics from using the issue as part of a broader argument that Obama is insufficiently traditional or insufficiently patriotic. His supporters say the attacks are distractions from substantive debates over Iraq, health care, and the economy.

The latest controversy involves William Ayers, a former member of the Weather Underground, a radical anti-war group responsible for bombings decades ago. Ayers later became a professor and education activist in Chicago. Obama has served with Ayers on civic and education-related boards, and Ayers once hosted a small political gathering for Obama early in his career.

Obama again distanced himself from Ayers’ past actions.

**OBAMA:**  
The violent acts committed by the Weather Underground happened when I was a child, and I have condemned them. My relationship with Mr. Ayers is not close. I know him as someone involved in education issues in Chicago. That does not mean I endorse his past, and I don’t.

**REPORTER:**  
Obama’s campaign says the connection is being exaggerated for political purposes. Opponents argue it raises questions about judgment and associations. The issue has gained traction in conservative media and could continue into the general election if Obama becomes the Democratic nominee.

For Obama, the challenge is balancing rebuttal and redirection. He does not want these controversies to define his campaign, but ignoring them risks allowing critics to shape the narrative.

At today’s event, Obama tried to turn the questions back toward his central theme: that voters are tired of what he calls the old politics of division.

**OBAMA:**  
People are hurting. They’re worried about their jobs, their homes, their health care, their kids going to college. That’s what this election should be about. If we spend all our time trading rumors and questioning who loves America, then we’re not solving the problems Americans sent us here to solve.

**ANCHOR:**  
So the Obama campaign is attempting to put these controversies behind it, but as the race intensifies, questions over identity, patriotism, and associations continue to test the candidate’s ability to control his message.

**REPORTER:**  
That’s right. Obama’s advisers believe these attacks are meant to raise doubts about him among undecided voters. Their strategy is to answer directly, then pivot back to policy and the larger argument for change. Whether that works may depend on how much voters see these issues as legitimate concerns — or simply campaign-season distractions.

**ANCHOR:**  
CNN’s campaign coverage continues after the break.
